steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Last time we learned to ‘see’ linear combinations: walk along one vector, then another, and so on.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: But we shouldn’t skip the formal definition

factData.title: Definition of a Linear Combination
factData.text: A linear combination of vectors v₁, v₂, …, vₖ is any vector of the form α₁v₁ + α₂v₂ + … + αₖvₖ, where the α’s are real numbers.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Now is the time to address some common misconceptions…

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Suppose we combine three vectors u=(2,1), v=(-1,3), and w=(6,0). Where can we get to?

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Right — no matter how many 2D vectors you add, you stay in 2D.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Okay, so if I take three vectors in 3D, do I automatically span all of 3D?

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: It depends on the choice of vectors. Sometimes they span the whole space, but sometimes they trap you on a line or a plane.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Can you give me an example of 3D vectors that only span a line?

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Why do these three vectors only span a line?

answers.text: Because they are in different directions.
They’re just different lengths of the same direction.
answers.feedback: So any combination of them is still on that line.

answers.text: Because just three vectors can’t span 3D.

steps.speaker: Assistant
steps.message: Ah, so more vectors don’t always mean more freedom.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: This idea — that vectors ‘add nothing new’ — is when linear dependence comes in.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Next time, we’ll learn how to check dependence and independence systematically.

steps.speaker: Teacher
steps.message: Now let’s finish with a short review. Select all correct statements:

answers.text: A linear combination always gives a vector
Linear combinations of 2D vectors can give 3D vectors
A span is the set of all linear combinations of given vectors
More vectors always mean more freedom
